orientation.summary: This is Alaska's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive 10-year conservation plan produced by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) for species of greatest conservation need (SGCN). The document is strongly climate-aware, devoting a full chapter (Chapter 7) to climate change as a threat, with extensive discussion of observed and projected effects on Alaska's wildlife and habitats including range shifts, marine heat waves, sea ice loss, and permafrost thaw. The document acknowledges climate-driven range shifts explicitly and repeatedly, referencing poleward movement of species, northward expansion of subarctic species into Arctic regions, treeline advance, and shrub expansion into tundra. Analysis is primarily narrative synthesis of published literature and partner knowledge; the document does not itself run climate models or species distribution models, though it references results of prior work (heatmaps of SGCN richness, GAP analysis range maps) and the Alaska Species Ranking System (ASRS) as a vulnerability/ranking tool. Conservation actions emphasize monitoring, research, partnerships, invasive species control, habitat management, and multistate collaboration but do not include explicit assisted migration or range-shift-specific translocations.

evidence_index.text: The number of species is not static. New species are still being discovered in Alaska, and as the climate changes, more species' ranges are expanding to the north (Parmesan and Yohe 2003).

there is a well-documented poleward shift of many well-studied plant and animal species on all continents and in most major oceans (Perry et al. 2005, Parmesan 2006, Hitch and Leberg 2007, LaSorte and Thompson 2007).

Subarctic seabirds, fishes, and marine mammals are shifting northward into Arctic regions in response to increased water temperatures, changes in water mass distributions, decreased extent and duration of ice cover, and altered prey communities (Stafford et al. 2022).
Climate change in the Arctic exceeds the mean global rate (Sweeney et al. 2023, Zhou et al. 2024). It is expected to add conservation challenges to species and habitats (Moon et al. 2024).

Impacts at higher trophic levels included mass mortality, shifts in distribution, and colony-wide reproductive failures of Common Murres (Arimitsu et al. 2021, Piatt et al. 2020, Renner et al. 2024); mass mortality of fin and humpback whales (Savage 2017); and sharply reduced humpback whale reproductive success (Gabriele et al. 2022).

The changes precipitated a range of shifts in the zooplankton community (Kimmel et al. 2023, Overland et al. 2024); movement of predatory fish into the northern Bering Sea (Stevenson and Lauth 2019); and declines in juvenile snow crab, impacting the southeastern Bering Sea snow crab population (Fedewa et al. 2020, Szuwalski et al. 2023).

Overall trends point to continued warming and a possible transition of the rich and unique ecosystems to novel states rather than a return to past conditions (NOAA 2021, Overland et al. 2024, Renner et al. 2024).

Owing to the high connectivity of habitats, wildlife in Alaska may be more resilient to climate change than wildlife in other parts of the United States where habitat fragmentation by human activities is more extensive (Vynne et al. 2021).

For example, wildlife in Alaska may be able to more easily move to higher elevations or latitudes (e.g., Tape et al. 2016, 2018, Mizel et al. 2016) as their habitats change because there are fewer anthropogenic barriers to dispersal.

Climate-related shifts in distribution or abundance may have ecosystem-wide effects, especially as new species immigrate or emigrate. Wildlife managers, therefore, need to adapt management strategies to account for the effects of a changing climate

Alaska is warming at two to three times the global average (Markon et al. 2018, Ballinger et al. 2023), and the Arctic is warming at four times the global average (Rantanen et al. 2022). Annual average temperatures since 1971 have increased by approximately 2.4°F in the Southeast biogeographic region to approximately 6.2°F in the Northern biogeographic region

Daily high temperatures exceeded normal temperatures by more than 20°F, resulting in uncharacteristically severe disturbances, such as the Swan Lake Fire on the Kenai Peninsula (Jandt and York 2021) and fish kills from thermal stress in multiple areas of the state
In recent years, uncharacteristic rain-on-snow events across the Arctic have been observed, negatively impacting forage and habitat availability for mammals and resident birds (Serreze et al. 2021).

evidence_index.text: warmer temperatures and milder winters have led to an increase in the severity of spruce beetle (Dendroctonus rufipennis) outbreaks (Dell and Davis 2019), negatively impacting habitat quality and suitability for some forest-dwelling species

Some emerging infectious diseases in wildlife are linked to climate change, and there is evidence that the spread and prevalence of some diseases is increasing (Van Hemert et al. 2014). Warming ocean waters and marine heat waves, such as the one that affected the North Pacific Ocean during 2014-2016, have facilitated the spread of diseases.

Climate change can have complex effects on wildlife because interactions among many variables, such as temperature, precipitation, habitat availability, ecosystem processes, and species interactions, are complicated and difficult to predict. For example, combined with the changes in habitat and seasonality described above, changes in the timing of spring leafout of vegetation or other historically reliable indicators can create a 'mismatch' for migratory bird flight timing and food availability.

Decreased winter sea ice cover in the Bering Sea due to climate change is likely to affect populations of these eiders over the next two decades. ADF&G and partners are conducting research to understand the effects of the changing climate on this SGCN.

In Alaska, climate change is altering habitat availability-sometimes rapidly-through reductions in sea ice and glacial extent, as well as changes in shrub cover and hydrology (Chapter 7). However, the high level of habitat connectivity in Alaska's large and relatively undisturbed terrestrial ecosystems will likely allow many SGCN to transition to other suitable habitats as they develop in a changing environment.
The changing climate will cause gradual shifts in the types of wetland and aquatic habitats available to Alaska's fish and wildlife (see the 'Climate Change' section in Chapter 7).

This is expected to result in a gradual transition of wetlands to more well-drained upland habitats during the next 10-20 years, particularly in the Central, Southcentral, and Southwest biogeographic regions
assisting species with low dispersal capabilities in colonizing newly available suitable habitats that develop as a result of climate change.

For species projected to lose habitat, there is a need to identify future habitats and hotspots of occurrence that could serve as climate change refugia and contribute to resiliency of SGCN. This can be done by comparing current and projected future habitat values and identifying physical factors and ecosystem processes that influence current and future habitat suitability (Stralberg et al. 2020, Raiho et al. 2022).

Range shifts have already been documented in some species groups (Mizel et al. 2016, Tape et al. 2016, Baltensperger et al. 2024), and long-term monitoring of SGCN distribution and abundance will help prioritize species for conservation and management actions.

Climate change is likely the most impactful threat to wildlife in Alaska because it affects habitats across the state and, for migratory species, where those species migrate and overwinter outside the state. Species that inhabit the northern edge of the continent or depend on sea ice are likely to be the most vulnerable to climate change because their niche is both shifting and disappearing.

Robust monitoring will be essential during this time period to identify which species are likely to be resilient to climate change and which will require additional management to support their resilience.

The ASRS evaluation process combines in-depth literature review with information provided by specialists and requires clear documentation for rankings while allowing for specialist opinion when some information is lacking. Rankings are updated with new information that can impact changes in status.

To rank risk levels for terrestrial vertebrates and marine mammals, we used a combination of two ASRS categories: Status and Biological. The Status category assigns a score to each species that quantifies current trends in population size and distribution in Alaska. The Biological category assigns a score that assesses a species' vulnerability based on population size, range size, and population concentration in Alaska. It also assesses life history characteristics, including reproductive potential and ecological specialization.

evidence.text: USFWS has eradicated invasive species and restored over one million acres on nearly 50 islands in the Aleutians, including the removal of introduced fox populations from 45 islands. On two Aleutian islands (Nizki and Alaid) that were studied before and after fox removal, the numbers of 12 waterbird and seabird species increased from 5,000 prior to fox removal to 14,000 after removal was complete (Byrd et al. 1994).

Without invasive northern pike suppression efforts, Chinook salmon would likely be extirpated from the Alexander Creek drainage (Bradley et al. 2022). ADF&G has also conducted research on migratory species, including the Black Oystercatcher and Rusty Blackbird, two species of continental concern for which breeding populations in Alaska were productive and appeared stable

projects: Fox eradication on Aleutian Islands (Nizki and Alaid): Before-and-after monitoring showed seabird and waterbird numbers increased from 5,000 to 14,000 after fox removal, demonstrating efficacy of invasive species eradication for native wildlife recovery.

Rat eradication from Hawadax (Rat) Island: Successful removal of rats from a 7,100-acre Aleutian island led to ecosystem recovery, providing evidence that island invasive rodent removal can benefit native bird populations.

Invasive northern pike suppression in Alexander Creek: Data-supported action showing pike removal prevented extirpation of Chinook salmon from the drainage, providing evidence for efficacy of pike suppression in protecting native salmonids.

orientation.summary: This is the 2015 Alabama State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a 10-year update of the state's Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Strategy, produced by the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (ADCNR). The document acknowledges climate change as one of many threats to SGCN and key habitats, with a dedicated section on 'Climate Change and Severe Weather' covering habitat shifting, droughts, temperature extremes, and storms, and a summary table rating habitat vulnerability to climate change. However, climate change is not the central organizing framework — habitat loss, fragmentation, water quality, and dam construction dominate. The document references range shifts in a very limited way (sea level rise, northward/upslope community shifts mentioned briefly), and references the TNC resilience framework and several climate vulnerability references in its literature cited. The document performs its own species/habitat assessments, priority area mapping, and conservation action planning; it cites external climate vulnerability literature but does not itself apply vulnerability models or species distribution models to SGCN.

evidence_index.text: Species and populations likely to have greater sensitivities to climate change include those with highly specialized habitat requirements, native species already near temperature limits or having other narrow environmental tolerances, currently isolated, rare, or declining populations with poor dispersal abilities

Species with these traits will be even more vulnerable if they have a small population, a low reproductive rate, long generation times, low genetic diversity, or are threatened by other factors (Bagne et al. 2014, Gardali et al. 2012, Johnson, 2014, Lankford et al. 2014, NFWPCAP 2014, Small-Lorenz et al. 2013).
Major changes in habitat composition and location may include sea level rise and northward or upslope shifting of natural community types.

Sea level rise poses significant threats to coastal ecosystems that may become inundated, resulting in habitat changes and losses, and adverse impacts to species or communities that depend on these habitats.

It is generally considered by climate scientists that coastal ecological resources are likely to be among the most sensitive to the changing climate, and that the climate change impacts to ecosystems over the next few decades will be most marked in the coastal zones (Frumhoff et al. 2007; Karl et al. 2009, IPCC 2007).

Periods in which temperatures exceed or go below the normal range of variation may manifest as heat waves, cold spells, and oceanic temperature changes, all of which can affect the distribution of species. Those occurring at the southern periphery of their range, such as the Wood Frog and Cerulean Warbler, may be most affected.

Urbanization and forest fragmentation are inextricably linked to the effects of climate change, because the dispersal and migration of forest plants and animals are disrupted by development and roads.

The Nature Conservancy (Anderson. et al. 2014) estimated the resilience to climate change of distinct geophysical settings across the southeastern United States (Figure 3-27). The methodology identified sites for all the geophysical settings that are likely to retain species and functions longer under a changing climate

Critical habitats-those areas in which targeted species can persist and/or relocate over time-may provide a refuge from climate change impacts and become high-priority candidates for acquisition and enhanced conservation efforts.

Research can be conducted to identify structurally diverse and species-rich habitats as well as important movement corridors. Monitoring for new invasive plants, insects, and other pests may be implemented.

Cool-water streams and cold-water fish habitat can be incorporated into buffer strategies in order to conserve connected water bodies and protect vegetative canopies over streams to help reduce impacts of warming temperatures.

This protection mosaic has conserved important populations of SGCN, such as the Alabama Beach Mouse, and their habitats. However, this reserve system was established during a time when the challenge of climate change and resulting shifting coastlines and habitats was not fully appreciated.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 draft revision of Arkansas's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive biodiversity conservation framework covering 520 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and their habitats across the state. The document treats climate change as one of several major threats but primarily frames it as a background stressor rather than a central organizing principle; climate science is engaged most substantively in Chapter 5 (regional perspective), which includes a dedicated 'Arkansas Climate Resiliency' section referencing CMIP6 models, SSP scenarios, CCVI assessments, and ecological niche models applied to Arkansas SGCN. Range shifts are discussed explicitly (species may shift distributions under climate change; warm-adapted species may dominate; cold-adapted species may shift), and both vulnerability tools (CCVI) and niche models are referenced as applied to the plan's focal species. Conservation opportunity areas (COAs) with spatial maps are identified. The document performs its own vulnerability summaries using CCVI and niche model results harvested from literature; it does not conduct new modeling but incorporates prior results into management discussion.

However, the Fifth National Climate Assessment (NCA5) used newly developed climate projections created with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs)

The climate projections used in the NCA5 were created using global climate models from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) that were statistically downscaled to translate large scale changes in the climate under a given SSP or GWL to local scales for impact assessment and planning

Three of the SSPs used with the new climate models from the CMIP6 correspond to three of the RCPs used with past global climate models from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) in their overall forcing levels (SSP1-2.6 corresponds with RCP2.6, SSP2-4.5 with RCP4.5, and SSP5-8.5 with RCP8.5)

orientation.summary: This is Arizona's 2022 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), titled the Arizona Wildlife Conservation Strategy (AWCS), produced by the Arizona Game and Fish Department. It is a comprehensive statewide conservation strategy covering Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need, and Conservation Opportunity Areas (COAs). The document treats climate change as a serious and growing threat throughout, dedicating sections within each habitat profile to 'Conservation in the Context of Climate Change.' It references range shifts explicitly in the context of climate adaptation strategies (e.g., facilitating range shifts via connectivity improvements, assisted migration, and refugia protection), but performs no original climate or range-shift modeling itself—it references external projections and frameworks. The document's analysis is primarily narrative and action-planning oriented, drawing on prior assessments and AFWA guidelines.

orientation.summary: This is the second edition of the Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Strategy (CWCS) for the Territory of American Samoa, produced by the Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources (DMWR), covering both terrestrial and marine fauna. The document is broadly climate-aware, treating climate change as a significant and increasing threat to wildlife and marine habitats, particularly coral reefs and coastal species, but it does not perform its own climate modeling or vulnerability assessment — it acknowledges these as needed and proposes them as future priority actions. Range shifts are not a primary conceptual framing; the document instead focuses on population decline, habitat degradation, and species vulnerability to multiple stressors. References to distributional change are mostly implicit (species near range boundaries, distribution shifts tied to bleaching and warming), and connectivity is addressed primarily in the context of larval transport and island-to-island movement rather than climate-driven range shifts. Climate change is treated as a compound threat to existing habitats and species, not as a driver of geographic redistribution.

orientation.summary: California's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP 2025) is a comprehensive statewide biodiversity conservation plan produced by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW). The document is strongly climate-change-aware throughout, with a dedicated section on climate vulnerability (Section 2.5) discussing observed and projected changes in temperature, precipitation, wildfire, sea level rise, and ocean conditions. The document explicitly engages with range shifts—describing species moving to higher latitudes or elevations, shifting habitats, and the role of connectivity in facilitating climate-driven movement—particularly in the connectivity appendix (Appendix H), the statewide vulnerability section, and individual province chapters. The document performs its own analysis in identifying SGCN, ranking conservation targets, and compiling statewide connectivity maps; it references and substantively incorporates published vulnerability assessments and connectivity models developed by CDFW and partners rather than running primary climate modeling.

orientation.summary: This is a 2025 draft State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) for the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), covering terrestrial and marine species and habitats across the 14-island Mariana Archipelago. The document is climate-aware, explicitly identifying long-term environmental shifts (warming, ocean acidification, sea level rise, altered precipitation, intensified typhoons, coral bleaching) as threats to SGCN and habitats. Range shifts are not the primary framing; the document instead addresses climate-driven habitat degradation and species vulnerability primarily through its resiliency assessment framework (NatureServe CCVI 4.0 and Thomas Framework) applied to SGCN. Most climate analysis draws on external sources (East West Center 2021 report), while the document performs its own species resiliency assessments internally. Conservation actions are largely organized around habitat protection, invasive species management, monitoring, and multi-island coordination, with limited explicit range-shift-specific management actions.

The Thomas Framework is a six stage scoring criteria which takes into consideration possible species benefits from changing environmental conditions (e.g. range expansion).

orientation.summary: This is Colorado's 2015 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive statewide wildlife conservation planning document produced by Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW). The document is strongly climate-aware, explicitly discussing climate change as a significant threat to most habitat types and many SGCN. It references range shifts explicitly in several contexts (e.g., habitat shifting and alteration, species adjusting elevation or latitude), and performs an original habitat-based climate change vulnerability assessment (Appendix F) covering 13 habitat types. The document references climate vulnerability tools including NatureServe's CCVI applied to rare plants, and uses GCM-based mid-century climate projections under RCP6 to assess habitat exposure. Actions are organized by species and habitat with threat/conservation action tables, but the plan is primarily a strategic prioritization document rather than a highly operationalized implementation plan.

evidence_index.text: Climate projections for Colorado are generally in agreement that the state will experience temperatures that are 2-5 °F warmer than current temperatures by mid-century. Projections for future precipitation are variable, ranging from very dry to approximately 10% wetter than current conditions.

As temperatures increase and precipitation regimes change, suitable climatic conditions for species and/or habitats may shift in elevation or latitude. There is the potential for this to result in different tree, shrub, and understory species dominating the landscape. In the future, we may see novel plant communities emerge or significant loss of current communities.

Understanding why species and ecosystems are vulnerable or potentially less resilient is a critical first step in developing effective conservation strategies. This vulnerability is based on sensitivity, exposure, and the ability to adapt.

The primary components of this method are projected exposure to climate change, sensitivity of the species or ecosystem to expected changes, and the adaptive capacity of the species or ecosystem to respond to changes (Figure 1).
Species with low adaptive capacity such as those with specialized habitat needs or limited dispersal ability face higher vulnerability to these changes.

The sagebrush habitat within Colorado does not appear to be particularly vulnerable to climate change, some sagebrush obligate species -most notably the Gunnison sage-grouse -are thought to be extremely vulnerable. However, the habitat is not expected to be limited by lack of cooler habitat, since it can move to adjacent higher elevations.
Preliminary results of our climate change vulnerability assessment suggest that lodgepole may be moderately vulnerable through mid-century.

Our climate change vulnerability analysis (Appendix F) indicated that alpine habitats are moderately vulnerable to the effects of climate change by mid-century. Snowpack patterns are important for this habitat. Thus, if Colorado experiences an increase in winter precipitation, alpine areas may be able to withstand some increase in temperature, at least in the short term, and especially in areas where it is difficult for trees to advance. At a longer time frame, however, alpine is likely to largely disappear from Colorado.

Under warmer conditions, spruce-fir is likely to expand into alpine areas, but the response would be slow. The lower distributional limit of this habitat is likely to move higher under warmer, drier conditions.

orientation.summary: This is Connecticut's 2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive multi-chapter planning document produced by CT DEEP. The document is strongly engaged with climate change throughout, framing 'shifting environmental conditions' as the top threat to Connecticut's SGCN across nearly all taxonomic groups. Range shifts are explicitly discussed — including distributional changes in fish communities in Long Island Sound, range contractions for cold-water species, phenological mismatches, sea turtle range expansions, and the need for climate refugia and connectivity — but are treated mostly as threats to manage rather than as a framework the document itself models. The document references external studies and regional analyses (especially Burgio et al. 2024, Staudinger et al. 2024, Karmalkar et al. 2024) that underpin its assessments; it does not perform its own quantitative niche or climate modeling. The document proposes the Resist-Accept-Direct (RAD) framework and Resistance-Resilience-Transformation (RRT) frameworks explicitly, creates spatially explicit Conservation Opportunity Area maps using Zonation software with habitat suitability models for 14 SGCN, and includes a new Conservation Action Tracker tool.

document_meta.title: District of Columbia Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP 2015)

orientation.summary: This is the 2015 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) for the District of Columbia, a highly urbanized jurisdiction with unique wildlife management challenges. The document is strongly climate-aware: Chapter 5 is devoted to climate change vulnerability assessments, covering regional projections (temperature, precipitation, sea-level rise), habitat vulnerability analyses, and species-level vulnerability assessments using the NatureServe CCVI. Range shifts are explicitly discussed—particularly species at range margins that may shift northward or be extirpated—and the document frames climate change as a major long-term threat requiring proactive management. The plan performs its own spatial analyses (habitat condition mapping, COA designation, meadow restoration prioritization, SLAMM modeling) while also drawing heavily on external sources (Tree Atlas, regional climate projections, NatureServe CCVI scores, MCCS/NWF habitat vulnerability reports). Partnerships and monitoring are required SWAP elements and are addressed, though funding is described as limited.

evidence_index.text: Beyond the proximate threats of urban development and land use, climate change will affect nearly every aspect of natural resource management, land use planning, and future development in the long term.

Through SWAP 2015, DDOE seeks to conserve the wildlife and habitats of the nation's capital by focusing on ecosystem-based wildlife resource management actions that address the unique issues that wildlife face in an urban city and the significant challenge of climate change.

A fine-scale climate change vulnerability assessment was performed. Climate, precipitation, and soil moisture were modeled to predict changes in vegetative habitats and how those changes would impact certain SGCN. Results showed that sea level rise and changes in soil moisture will impact vulnerable habitats, such as emergent wetlands, upland forests, and vernal pools.
As the climate continues to change and become further unstable, it is expected to see shifts in species ranges such as in the case of the green tree frog.

As sea levels rise, marshes can be inundated and converted to shallow open water habitats or non-tidal and brackish wetlands may convert to higher salinity marshes. As a result, vegetative composition will change, affecting the wildlife species that depend on these habitats.
Vernal pools will likely be impacted by higher temperatures and longer durations between rain events, which will directly, negatively impact the populations that depend on these pools.

There is potential for the District to experience an increase in frequency, magnitude, and duration of heat waves (Meehl and Tebaldi 2004). Winter minimum temperatures are projected to rapidly rise, reducing the frequency of extremely cold days. Such, increases in temperature will negatively affect wildlife habitats and SGCN.

Warming temperatures will also lead to changes in plant phenology, as has already been observed (Primack et al. 2004, Miller-Rushing and Primack 2008). These changes may have significant impacts on ecosystems by changing existing natural land cover types and by allowing for the spread of pests into previously unaffected regions.

orientation.summary: This is the 2015 Delaware Wildlife Action Plan (DEWAP), a State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) produced by the Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control, Division of Fish and Wildlife. The document covers Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), their key habitats, threats, and conservation actions across Delaware. It is moderately climate-aware: Chapter 3 includes a dedicated section on climate change as a threat, discussing sea level rise, temperature projections, habitat shifting, and storm intensification, with references to Delaware-specific downscaled climate projections. However, the document does not apply formal climate models, SDMs, or connectivity models to its focal species. Range shifts are discussed implicitly in the context of climate impacts (northward species shifts noted as an observed trend nationally/regionally) but are not a central organizing theme. The document references prior studies and regional planning efforts rather than performing original range-shift analysis.

orientation.summary: This is Florida's 2019 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive statewide wildlife conservation document produced by the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The plan addresses climate change as one of several major threats to Florida's 690 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and their habitats, noting Florida's particular vulnerability due to its low elevation, extensive coastline, and sea level rise exposure. Climate-driven range shifts are referenced multiple times in the context of habitat and species responses to sea level rise, temperature changes, and altered hydrology, but the document performs limited original climate analysis itself—it references an external FWC guide ('A Guide to Climate Change Adaptation for Conservation,' FWC 2016a) for vulnerability details. Actions proposed related to climate include identifying migration corridors, conducting climate vulnerability assessments, and supporting adaptive management, but these are largely aspirational or delegated to future work.

orientation.summary: The 2015 Georgia State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a comprehensive wildlife conservation strategy produced by the Georgia Department of Natural Resources Wildlife Resources Division, covering 640 high-priority species and habitats across five ecoregions of the state. The document is broadly aware of climate change, dedicating a technical team and an entire subsection (Section V) to climate change adaptation, treating it as an 'emerging issue' that has become 'a central and defining wildlife conservation issue' since 2005. It references range shifts explicitly—noting species may move northward or to higher elevations—and discusses habitat connectivity as a strategy to support such movement. Most analysis is drawn from external sources (published studies, regional vulnerability assessments, other agencies' tools), though the document summarizes findings and lists specific conservation actions. The document uses the IPCC vulnerability framework (sensitivity, exposure, adaptive capacity) by reference but does not perform original quantitative analyses itself.

orientation.summary: The 2025 Guam State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a comprehensive biodiversity conservation strategy for Guam, a US territory in Micronesia, prepared by the Department of Agriculture Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources (DAWR) in collaboration with the University of Guam. The document addresses 128 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems, with primary threats dominated by the brown tree snake and invasive species. Climate change is acknowledged as an escalating threat and addressed more explicitly than in the 2015 revision, with references to impacts on species distributions, coral bleaching, sea level rise, and habitat degradation, but the document performs no original climate modeling or vulnerability assessments — it references such tools as aspirational future activities. Range shifts are referenced in a limited, mostly qualitative way, primarily in the context of changing species distributions and habitat suitability under climate change, with no systematic application of range-shift science.

evidence_index.text: Across the Pacific, there is clear evidence of rising air and sea surface temperatures, sea-level rise, increased frequency and duration of droughts, saltwater intrusion into freshwater lenses, shifting habitat and species distributions, and altered ocean chemistry.

Loss and migration of forest ecosystems (Grecni et al., 2020); Elevated extinction risk for native species (Grecni et al., 2020); More frequent coral bleaching events (Cipolla, 2021); Intensified threats to marine ecosystems (Grecni et al., 2020)
Climate change effects, including ocean acidification and increased frequency and severity of weather events
Changing precipitation patterns and warming temperatures are affecting the range of plant and animal species, pushing them into smaller or less suitable habitats with limited access to resources.
Species with low adaptive capacity such as those with specialized habitat needs or limited dispersal ability face higher vulnerability to these changes.

In supporting our SGCN, it is vital that we work towards long-term ecosystem resilience with proactive management, vulnerability assessments, habitat restoration and management, invasive species control, and climate-smart conservation planning.
Climate change is now addressed more explicitly in this plan. Anticipated impacts to Guam's wildlife, ecosystems, and natural resources require focused, adaptive management.
Warming sea temperatures lead to coral bleaching, weakening reef structures and reducing habitat for fish and other marine species.
Ocean acidification further disrupts coral health and growth, negatively impacting biodiversity that communities depend on for food and livelihoods.
Climate change further impacts mangrove systems and reduces the availability of freshwater through saltwater contamination of aquifers.
Freshwater resources are at risk from altered watershed dynamics and reduced rainfall, impacting the wetlands and streams that support our aquatic plants and animals.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 update to Hawai'i's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), produced by the Hawai'i Department of Land and Natural Resources (DLNR) and submitted to USFWS by October 1, 2025. The document is a comprehensive state-level biodiversity conservation plan covering over 1,400 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine environments. Climate change is treated as a significant and growing threat throughout the plan, with an entire subsection dedicated to 'Ecological Consequences of Climate Change' and a dedicated sub-chapter on 'Species Vulnerability Assessments in Response to Changing Climate.' Range shifts are discussed primarily in the context of mosquito-borne disease spreading upslope due to warming, but are not framed as a primary focus of management strategy. The plan synthesizes information from existing recovery plans, management strategies, and monitoring programs rather than performing new quantitative analyses.

document_meta.title: Iowa Wildlife Action Plan (IWAP) 2025 Draft Comprehensive Revision

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 comprehensive revision of Iowa's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), covering the state's species of greatest conservation need (SGCN) across all taxa, their habitats, threats, and conservation actions. The document acknowledges climate change as a significant threat to Iowa's wildlife throughout, particularly in Chapter 5's threat taxonomy (scoring climate change as 'Very High' for most taxa), and briefly discusses changing temperature and precipitation regimes, shifting plant community distributions, and phenological changes as climate-related concerns. The document does not perform its own range-shift analysis but references climate-driven distributional change in passing (e.g., as plant ranges shift, wildlife communities will change), and lists climate under 'Changes in Physical and Chemical Regimes' as causing range shifts. The plan's primary focus is habitat conservation, species monitoring, funding, and partnerships rather than climate-shift science, and it performs no niche modeling, vulnerability modeling, or climate modeling of its own—though it does mention species distribution models developed in partnership with Iowa State University from MSIM data.

orientation.summary: This is Illinois's 2015 Wildlife Action Plan Implementation Guide (an update to the 2005 Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Plan & Strategy, formally amended in 2022), a statewide conservation planning document organized around seven habitat-based Campaigns (Farmland and Prairie, Forest and Woodland, Green Cities, Invasive Species, Lake Michigan, Streams, and Wetlands). The document acknowledges climate change as a threat multiplier, particularly in the Streams and Invasive Species campaigns, but its overall posture is primarily focused on habitat management, invasive species control, and Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) recovery rather than climate adaptation. Range shifts are referenced tangentially—species moving through urban areas in response to changing climate is noted once in the Green Cities section, and the Streams campaign explicitly applies NatureServe's CCVI to Illinois aquatic SGCN. The document performs its own vulnerability assessment synthesis (citing Walk et al. 2011 CCVI results) and references climate change models/projections (Hall 2012; Staudinger et al. 2015) but does not itself run climate models; it primarily references externally produced analyses to frame threats.

orientation.summary: This is Indiana's 2015 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a revision of the original 2005 Comprehensive Wildlife Strategy, produced by the Indiana Division of Fish and Wildlife. The document takes a habitat-based, regional conservation planning approach for Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across six planning regions. Climate change is acknowledged as a threat but receives only modest, non-specific treatment — it is consistently ranked in the lower tier of threats (often 6th-10th among 11 categories) across regions and taxa, and the document does not perform climate modeling, vulnerability assessments, or range-shift analysis itself. Range shifts are not explicitly framed as a central concern; occasional references to 'shifting and alteration of habitats due to climate change' and 'shifting seasons/phenology' appear in threat tables, but these are survey-derived rankings rather than the plan's own analysis. The plan's primary analysis involves statewide surveys of species experts and habitat managers, landscape-level habitat suitability models (moved to appendix), and Conservation Opportunity Area (COA) designation.

orientation.summary: The 2022 Kansas State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is the third edition of Kansas's comprehensive wildlife conservation plan, replacing the 2015 edition. It covers 429 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across three conservation regions (Shortgrass Prairie, Central Mixed-Grass Prairie, Eastern Tallgrass Prairie) and identifies 13 priority habitats and Ecological Focus Areas (EFAs). The document treats climate change as one of eight statewide conservation issues and includes a dedicated section on climate change vulnerability assessment (Appendix 5/6) applying the NatureServe Climate Change Vulnerability Index (CCVI) to 83 SGCN. Range shifts are explicitly discussed as a consequence of climate change, including species distribution shifts, phenological changes, and decoupling of co-evolved interactions, but the plan's primary analytical work is qualitative; the CCVI application is the main quantitative tool applied to focal species. The plan does not use formal climate models or SDMs but references climate projections qualitatively; connectivity is discussed in both generic and climate-relevant contexts via the CHAT system.

evidence_index.text: Climate changes are likely to influence species and ecosystems by altering fundamental interactions with other species and the physical environment, potentially creating a cascade of impacts throughout ecosystems (Staudinger, et al. 2012).

Climate models predict changes in annual precipitation that vary geographically and temporally. The eastern half of the state could see increases in precipitation of up to 11 inches (28 cm) per year in the 2090-2099 timeframe. The west will likely see a drying climate in the short and long term, but there is a high level of disagreement between models.

Species are already being significantly impacted by climate change. Effects such as shifts in species distributions, changes in phenology of species, and de-coupling of co-evolved interactions have been documented.
Increasing temperatures may cause range shifts or contractions of flora and fauna. Species that have limited mobility or are unable to migrate may become extirpated or even extinct.
An increase of extreme events such as floods, droughts, heat waves, and severe storms are expected, which can alter species habitats by increasing wildfires, pests, diseases, and invasive species.

Individual species and habitats will have very different responses to climate change. Many species and habitats will be negatively affected by climate change and will require a special set of actions to ensure their survival. Some species may benefit from a changing climate and could expand their range or increase in abundance, requiring a separate set of actions.
In addition, the movement of species will create new communities of species for which there will be no previous examples and will require new management regimes.
As part of the SWAP revision a climate change vulnerability assessment was conducted on several SGCN. The methods and results of that work are summarized in Appendix 6.

Vulnerability to climate change has three principle components; sensitivity (innate characteristics of a species or system, considers tolerance to changes temp, precip, fire etc), exposure (extrinsic factors, magnitude and rate of change species/system experiences), and adaptive capacity (ability to accommodate with climate change impacts with minimal disruption).

evidence_index.text: Climate change vulnerability assessments provide two essential contributions to adaptation planning. Specifically, they help in: identifying which species or systems are likely to be more strongly affected by projected changes; and understanding why these resources are likely to be vulnerable, including the interaction between climate shifts and existing stressors.

orientation.summary: This is the 2023 second revision of Kentucky's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive statewide conservation document produced by the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR) covering 527 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across 9 taxonomic groups. The plan acknowledges climate change as a recognized global threat that compounds existing stressors to SGCN and their habitats, with a dedicated Climate Change appendix (APX 5.2) and a 'Strategy of Resilience' section outlining climate action items. However, the plan primarily focuses on species status, habitat description, threat identification, and conservation actions for species-level management, with climate change addressed generically as one of many threat categories. The plan performs its own original analysis (SGCN selection, COA delineation, habitat modeling) and references external analyses (SECAS Blueprint, TNC models) to inform management decisions. Range shifts are mentioned implicitly—species distributions, range contractions, and monitoring for distributional changes are documented—but the plan does not frame climate-driven range shifts as a central organizing concept.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 Louisiana State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive state-level wildlife conservation planning document produced by the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries (LDWF). The document is strongly climate-aware, dedicating an entire chapter (Chapter 10: Louisiana: A Regional Perspective) to climate change impacts, climate projections, and climate resilience, and explicitly engaging with vulnerability assessments (CCVI) and ecological niche models. Its posture toward range shifts is substantial: it discusses projected shifts in species distributions, climate exposure, and adaptive capacity, and references the Southeast Conservation Blueprint's connectivity/corridor analysis and resilience mapping. The document primarily synthesizes and incorporates prior analyses (CCVI scores, niche models, Southeast Conservation Blueprint) rather than performing new modeling itself. Conservation actions include spatially defined Conservation Opportunity Areas (COAs), habitat corridors, and specific species management actions, though explicit climate-driven range-shift facilitation actions are limited.

evidence_index.text: A species is considered vulnerable to climate change if it is both sensitive and exposed to climate change impacts (Williams et al. 2008). For example, a species may be exposed to climate change, because it experiences an impact like warmer stream temperatures; but if it is resilient to that change or able to disperse into new habitats, it may, ultimately, have low vulnerability.

orientation.summary: The 2015 Massachusetts State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a comprehensive statewide biodiversity conservation plan prepared by the Massachusetts Division of Fisheries and Wildlife, covering 570 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across 24 habitat types. The document has a strongly climate-aware posture, dedicating an entire chapter (Chapter 5) to climate change integration, including a Manomet-led Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment and a BioMap2 spatial conservation framework explicitly designed around climate change resilience. Range shifts are discussed across many habitat sections—species moving northward, habitats shifting, and trailing-edge contractions—but the treatment is primarily qualitative and relies heavily on the external Manomet/NWF vulnerability assessment rather than new modeling conducted for this plan. The plan performs its own BioMap2 spatial analysis and Key Sites identification, but quantitative range-shift modeling (SDMs, climate models) is referenced from external projects rather than performed internally.

evidence_index.text: Since the 2005 SWAP, response to climate change by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts has centered on developing a better understanding of how climate change is likely to impact SGCN and their habitats, including the adaptive capacity of these species and how they might respond to climate changes.

In 2010, the Manomet Center for Conservation Sciences, in Plymouth, MA, worked with the DFW to conduct a Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment of many of the habitats identified in the 2005 SWAP. This project was conducted under the leadership of Dr. Hector Galbraith, who used an expert elicitation approach to conduct the assessment. Staff members from the DFW were asked a series of questions regarding their expert opinions regarding how the SGCN species may react to various climate conditions. Climate change projections were derived using two emission scenarios.

Volume 2 -Habitat and Species Vulnerability. This volume reports the results of the work assessing the likely vulnerabilities of fish and wildlife and their habitats to climate change. The report addresses the following questions: How do the SWAP-targeted fish and wildlife habitats rank in terms of their likely comparative vulnerabilities to climate change? How will the representation of these habitats in Massachusetts be altered by a changing climate? Which vertebrate Species in Greatest Need of Conservation are likely to be most vulnerable to climate change?

Volume 3 -Habitat Management. This report provides at least partial answers to the second question: how valued ecological resources might be effectively managed as climatic conditions continue to change. What degree of confidence can be assigned to the above predictions?

orientation.summary: This is the 2025-2035 Maryland State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a draft state-level wildlife conservation planning document produced by the Maryland Department of Natural Resources (MD DNR). The document is comprehensive, covering species of greatest conservation need (SGCN), key wildlife habitats (KWHs), threats, and conservation actions for the 2025-2035 period. Climate change is explicitly recognized as a major threat throughout the document, with sea-level rise, saltwater intrusion, phenological mismatch, and range shifts mentioned in multiple sections. The document references range shifts explicitly as a climate-driven threat and management concern (species are expected to shift into or out of Maryland), and incorporates climate vulnerability as a selection criterion for SGCN. The document performs its own analysis through habitat mapping (SLAMM, HCN), threat-action prioritization matrices, and species assessments, while also heavily referencing external frameworks (RSGCN lists, NECASC syntheses, NEAFWA lexicon). It discusses connectivity (Maryland Habitat Connectivity Network) and sea-level rise adaptation (SLAMM/WAA modeling) as planning tools applied to the document's focal subjects.

orientation.summary: This is Michigan's 2025-2035 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive multi-chapter conservation plan covering 714 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across 18 habitat chapters. The document has a strong posture toward climate change as a pervasive threat, explicitly incorporating adaptive capacity assessments for all terrestrial focal species (using the Thurman et al. 2020 framework applied to ~400 Midwest SGCN) and climate vulnerability rankings for aquatic focal species (using habitat suitability models per Cooper et al. 2022, projecting distribution change by 2050). Range shifts are addressed throughout: multiple chapters discuss northward/elevational shifts, boreal refugia, snowshoe hare southern range contraction, golden-winged warbler northward shift, and species tracking climate. Actions are largely framed as habitat management, connectivity maintenance, and monitoring, with limited explicit assisted-migration or translocation actions. The plan references numerous external analyses (Hoving et al. 2013 CCVI, Cooper et al. 2022 SDMs, Thurman et al. 2020 AC tool) as applied to its focal species rather than performing new independent modeling, while also developing new AC assessments via Appendix 3.

orientation.summary: This is Minnesota's 2015-2025 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), produced by the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources. The document is strongly climate-aware throughout, framing climate change as a major stressor on habitats and SGCN and explicitly conducting a habitat climate change vulnerability assessment as part of the update process. Range shifts are referenced substantively—the plan notes species are already moving in response to climate change and designs the Wildlife Action Network partly to facilitate future range shifts. The document performs its own spatial analyses (GIS-based network mapping, Marxan runs, SGCN population ranking) and incorporates externally produced vulnerability assessments (Northwoods Climate Change Response Framework, various synthesis studies), but does not apply formal niche or climate models to project species distributions under future scenarios.

evidence_index.text: Minnesota's changing climate may also make it more difficult to effectively implement single-species management and is driving a greater focus on landscape-scale conservation. These changes are requiring conservation programs to prioritize work within connected habitat networks to facilitate species movement and adaptation
updating the plan involved conducting a habitat climate change vulnerability assessment and reviewing habitat and species vulnerability assessments and other information about the changing climate.

Species are already moving in response to climate change, and it is expected that the ranges of many more plant and animal species will shift and habitats will change. The Wildlife Action Network will facilitate adaptation to these changes by identifying core areas large enough to contain a diversity of ecotones and habitats to allow for local shifts (e.g., dry to mesic prairie), and connections to allow for species movements

As climate change becomes more pronounced, its effects will be both direct and indirect. Impacts from climate change in addition to those from other large-scale drivers will be synergistic; that is, multiple stressors will have an effect that is greater than what may be considered simply additive.

orientation.summary: This is Missouri's 2015 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a revision of the 2005 Comprehensive Wildlife Conservation Strategy, produced by the Missouri Department of Conservation. The document takes a habitat-based conservation approach across six primary habitat systems (Grassland/Prairie/Savanna, Forest/Woodland, Glade, Cave/Karst, Wetland, Rivers/Streams) and identifies Conservation Opportunity Areas (COAs) statewide. Climate change is acknowledged as an emerging threat, discussed in a brief section within Elements 3 and 4, with a notable sub-section summarizing findings from a 2014 Central Hardwoods vulnerability assessment (Brandt et al. 2014); the document does not itself perform climate modeling or vulnerability analysis but incorporates external results. Range shifts are mentioned implicitly — as species adapting to climate change via connectivity — and connectivity is highlighted as a mechanism to facilitate range adjustments, though no targeted range-shift actions are proposed. Partnerships and funding are well-documented throughout habitat system chapters, with numerous named partner organizations and cost-share mechanisms.

evidence_index.text: New threats continue to emerge such as new disease epidemics (e.g., chytrid fungus, white-nose syndrome), new chemical contaminants, and climate change.

Climate change is now widely recognized as a potential major threat to fish and wildlife and the habitat systems on which they depend. Climate change is a particularly challenging threat because of the ways in which it may interact with other threats, such as invasive species and disease, and because of the degree of uncertainty regarding the timing, seasonality, intensity and sometimes even direction of the impacts that may occur as a result of changing climate.

Many migratory species, such as mallards and other dabbling ducks, rely on temperature cues to signal northward and southward migration each year. As temperatures warm and precipitation patterns change, some wildlife species may experience a shift in breeding and migration dates, as has already been observed for North American wood warblers.
Changes in climate will also create additional management challenges as conditions become more favorable for invasive plant species not currently prevalent in the assessment area.

Increasing resilience has been identified as a primary method for minimizing the impacts of climate change on fish, forest and wildlife resources. Missouri's approach also promotes connectivity within and among habitat systems by prioritizing those areas that are larger, more intact, nearer to other conservation areas, and/or where there is more opportunity to expand conservation action. Improving connectivity will facilitate range adjustments that may occur in many species adapting to climate change.
Efforts to restore and maintain healthy habitat systems in these areas may result in more resilient habitat systems and floral and faunal communities.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 Mississippi State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive ten-year update developed by the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks. The document is strongly engaged with climate change throughout, particularly in Chapter 2 ('A Regional Perspective'), which includes detailed projections of future temperature extremes, drought, sea-level rise, and extreme precipitation using CMIP6-LOCA2 data under multiple SSP scenarios. The document incorporates vulnerability framing explicitly—referencing both CCVI and ecological niche models applied to Mississippi SGCN—and discusses range-shift concerns, habitat shifting, and connectivity at regional scales. Conservation actions are primarily habitat-based (COAs) with some specific climate-resilience language, but the plan does not operationalize climate-adaptive actions at the individual action-deadline level. The document performs its own synthesis of vulnerability data (drawing on prior CCVI assessments of 124 SGCN and ENM results for 159 SGCN from external studies) and incorporates the Southeast Conservation Blueprint connectivity analysis into its COA structure.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 draft revision of Montana's State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive state-level conservation planning document produced by Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks (FWP). It identifies 375 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and 52 Habitats of Greatest Conservation Need (HGCN) and outlines threats and conservation actions for each. The document is broadly aware of climate change as a driver of habitat degradation, altered phenology, and disease dynamics, with climate threats mentioned throughout the threats-and-actions tables under headings like 'Changes in Temperature Regimes' and 'Changes in Precipitation & Hydrological Regimes.' However, the document does not perform original climate modeling or vulnerability assessments; it references the Audubon 'Survival by Degrees' project for a handful of species and mentions climate risks qualitatively. Range shifts are discussed implicitly (species ranges expanding or contracting due to climate) in a few species accounts and in Chapter 8 on wildlife connectivity, which explicitly frames connectivity as enabling species to 'shift their ranges to track suitable conditions in response to changing environmental conditions.' The document performs its own analysis on habitat prioritization (via NVC mapping and spatial layers) and connectivity (Chapter 8) but relies on external literature and expert opinion rather than its own climate modeling or vulnerability scoring.

evidence_index.text: connectivity maintains genetic diversity by preventing populations from becoming isolated and allows species to shift their ranges to track suitable conditions in response to changing environmental conditions (Tabor et al. 2014).

Connectivity is fundamental for biodiversity conservation in an era of accelerating environmental change (Heller and Zavaleta 2009). As the landscape becomes increasingly fragmented, maintaining or restoring connectivity allows species to move safely between intact habitats to access necessary resources on a daily, seasonal, and annual basis.

Generally, strategies should include protecting lands that include intact habitats consisting of elevation gradients, diverse vegetation structure, functional disturbance regimes, a high proportion of native plant communities, topographic diversity, and water availability.

Habitat alteration due to rapid changes in hydrological and temperature regimes (e.g., changes in plant phenology creating a mismatch between arrival/emergence of wildlife/pollinators and flowering, seed production, reduced total production of vegetation due to hot and dry conditions and/or shifts in the timing/type of precipitation).

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 North Carolina State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive revision of the 2015 plan, produced by the NC Wildlife Resources Commission (NCWRC). The document extensively engages with climate change throughout, treating it as a major threat to species, habitats, and ecosystems across the state. Range shift science is referenced implicitly and explicitly across multiple chapters, particularly in discussions of coldwater fish moving upstream, species tracking suitable habitat, sea-level rise forcing coastal species inland, and high-elevation 'sky island' species facing extirpation. The plan primarily references analyses and assessments conducted by external partners (NCNHP, SECAS, climate scientists) rather than performing new range-shift modeling itself. Connectivity is discussed extensively as a conservation tool, and the plan includes a new GIS-based Conservation Opportunity Area analysis using the Southeast Conservation Blueprint.

document_meta.title: 2025 North Dakota State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP)

orientation.summary: The 2025 North Dakota State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a state-level wildlife conservation plan produced by the North Dakota Game and Fish Department (NDGF), serving as a 10-year blueprint for conserving 232 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and Species of Greatest Information Need (SGIN). The document engages substantively with climate change, dedicating a chapter section ('A Changing Climate') with climate projections to mid-century (2055) using CMIP5 GCMs and RCP scenarios, and includes multiple climate case studies examining range shifts of specific species (Dakota skipper, regal fritillary). The plan explicitly acknowledges climate-driven range shifts, phenological changes, and habitat transformation, and references climate scenario planning as a decision-making framework. Most analysis is referenced from external studies or the North Central Climate Adaptation Science Center rather than performed de novo by NDGF; however, the climate projections section represents a new synthesis prepared for the plan. Actions are primarily framed at the habitat level, with specific connectivity and spatial prioritization components (Focus Areas, KNWHA layer, resilient lands mapping).

evidence_index.text: Shifts in long-term temperatures and precipitation patterns, as well as the frequency of extreme events, and seasonality, is referred to as climate change. As these patterns shift, North Dakota could be impacted in several ways: more severe droughts, increased flooding, changes in growing season, etc.

Climate change can impact fish, wildlife, and the habitats they depend on in significant ways: shifts in species ranges, changes in behavioral or morphological traits, shifts in phenology, changes in species composition, increased pressure from non-native species, changes in predator/prey dynamics, etc.

A climate change scenario planning approach was used to select a set of plausible yet contrasting future conditions that encompass the range of critical uncertainties for the climate variables of interest in North Dakota (Lawrence et al., 2021; Miller et al., 2022).
A combination of 20 global circulation models CMIP5 (GCMs) for two emission scenarios (RCP4. 5 RCP 8.5) were used to select the representative potential climate futures

The time-period used for all climate projections is a mid-century planning period centered around 2055 (2040 -2069); this time period allows the incorporation of climate change into both short-term and long-term planning.

orientation.summary: This is Nebraska's third-edition State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), published in 2026 under the Nebraska Natural Legacy Project. The document is a comprehensive statewide biodiversity conservation plan covering Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), Biologically Unique Landscapes (BULs), priority watersheds, and recommended conservation actions across four ecoregions. The document acknowledges 'changing environmental conditions' driving species distribution shifts, phenological changes, and community disaggregation, with a dedicated section on 'Facilitate Species and Ecosystem Adaptation and Resiliency to Environmental Changes,' but does not use formal climate modeling, vulnerability assessments (CCVI), or species distribution models applied to focal subjects. The plan performs its own spatial prioritization (BULs, priority watersheds, demonstration sites) and species tiering, largely referencing climate-change-related threats qualitatively. Most analytical tools referenced (NatureServe ranking, PVA concepts) are applied for conservation status, not climate vulnerability per se.

evidence_index.text: Documented effects of a changing environment include: shifts in species distributions, changes in phenology of species, and decoupling of co-evolved interactions. In addition, these changes are expected to alter ecological processes such as fire regimes and hydrology, and exacerbate a number of existing stressors, such as habitat loss and fragmentation, pollution, and the spread of invasive species, pests, and pathogens.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 New Hampshire State Wildlife Action Plan (NH SWAP), a state-level SWAP covering the 2025-2035 planning period produced by the NH Fish and Game Department and partners. The document is substantially climate-aware, treating climate change as one of the top threats to SGCN and habitats, and dedicates a full section of Chapter 4 to climate change threats including projected temperature increases, sea-level rise, and species distributional responses. Range shifts are acknowledged explicitly (species moving poleward and upslope in response to climate) and referenced from the scientific literature, but the document performs no original range-shift modeling itself—it references the NE CASC Regional Climate Synthesis (Karmalkar et al., 2024) and other external analyses. Conservation actions reference climate refugia, connectivity, and climate projections but are largely programmatic rather than species-specific climate adaptation plans.

evidence_index.text: Watchlist: These are species that are presently secure in New Hampshire but are of concern elsewhere in the Northeast. Many of these species are suspected to be at risk due to emerging threats, such as climate change, that are affecting populations more strongly to our south.

In general, there are three broad responses of species to the impacts of climate change: move, adapt, or go extinct (Karmalkar et al., 2024). Recent research suggests that many taxa are already shifting higher in elevation and latitude, but results are inconsistent (Rubenstein et al., 2023), and marine taxa appear to track temperature shifts more closely than terrestrial species (Lenoir et al., 2020).

Some level of adaptation to a changing climate is likely for many species; however, species are more quickly shifting the timing of important parts of their life history (phenology; discussed in Appendix N) than they are their morphology or physiology. It remains to be seen if these shifts will be substantial enough to shield many species from serious population declines or extinction (Radchuk et al., 2019).

Predicting how species will respond to the changing climate depends on two things: how climate will change in the long- and short-term future, and how target species may directly respond to changing temperature and precipitation patterns, as well as indirect abiotic and biotic changes (Karmalkar et al., 2024). These predictions involve many dimensions of change, from physiological tolerances to phenology and interspecific interactions (Karmalkar et al., 2024).
Species with low adaptive capacity such as those with specialized habitat needs or limited dispersal ability face higher vulnerability to these changes.

The Northeast Climate Adaptation Science Center (NE CASC) led the development of a Regional Synthesis on Climate Data to inform the 2025 State Wildlife Action Plans in the Northeast U.S. (referred to as the Regional Climate Synthesis hereafter) (Karmalkar et al., 2024). orientation.summary: The 2022 Nevada State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a comprehensive statewide conservation plan produced by the Nevada Department of Wildlife (NDOW) covering 367 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) and 20 key habitats. The document treats climate change as a major overarching threat throughout, devoting a dedicated chapter section (Ch. 2) to climate change in Nevada with projections, and integrating climate change vulnerability assessments (via NatureServe's Habitat Climate Change Vulnerability Index, HCCVI) into each key habitat chapter (Ch. 4). Range shifts are addressed primarily at the habitat level through a Resist-Accept-Direct (RAD) framework, with some species-specific discussion. The document references prior analyses (e.g., LOCA CMIP5 downscaled projections, HCCVI assessments, species distribution models developed with NY Heritage) rather than performing entirely new modeling itself, though it does incorporate results from these tools into management decisions.

document_meta.title: Draft New York State Wildlife Action Plan (July 2025)

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 draft revision of the New York State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a comprehensive state-level biodiversity conservation planning document required for federal State Wildlife Grant eligibility. The document covers species of greatest conservation need (SGCN), habitats, threats, and conservation actions for New York. It engages substantially with climate change as a threat category (cited 661+ times across HPSGCN and SGCN), with specific discussion of temperature change, precipitation shifts, sea level rise, saltwater intrusion, and storms. Range shifts are not a primary organizing concept—the document focuses on habitat protection, threat assessment, and species-specific conservation actions—but climate-driven distributional change is implicitly present in discussions of habitat shifting, connectivity, and regional SGCN work. The document performs its own threat and action assessments but references external tools and reports (e.g., Audubon climate vulnerability reports, IPCC, Staudinger et al. 2024) for climate science rather than performing original climate modeling or vulnerability assessments internally.

evidence_index.text: Impacts in this category were cited as a threat to HPSGCN 290 times and to SGCN 371 times. This threat category includes habitat shifting and alteration, changes in geochemical regimes, changes in temperature regimes, changes in precipitation and hydrological regimes, and storms and severe weather.
The Level 3 threats cited most often were 'droughts' (158 species) and 'gradual temperature change' (80 species).

An increase or decrease in average air or water temperatures, changes to the timing and amount of precipitation events, increased salinity of coastal wetlands and tidal waters, increased unpredictability in the timing and severity of storms, and shifts in the composition of plant communities are some of the more frequently cited threats to SGCN in New York.

Higher ocean levels will increase the frequency and severity of damaging storm surges and shoreline flooding, permanently inundate some low-lying coastal areas with saltwater, and dramatically accelerate coastal erosion, threatening the ecologically important salt marshes and estuaries of Long Island.

evidence_index.text: wildlife health is defined by a population's ability to withstand stressors and challenges, such as climate change, habitat loss, the emergence of disease-causing agents, and other environmental, climatic and anthropogenic threats.

orientation.summary: Ohio's 2015 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a comprehensive state-level wildlife conservation document produced by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources Division of Wildlife. The plan takes a habitat-organized approach to conservation, covering 15 habitat categories and 405 Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN). It acknowledges climate change as an emerging threat throughout but dedicates a specific chapter (Chapter 5) to climate change, framing it as a threat that lags behind invasive species, habitat loss, and disease in current management attention. On range shifts specifically, the plan references northward distributional shifts, habitat connectivity, and species-level vulnerability assessments derived from external literature, but performs little original range-shift analysis itself—instead drawing on Staudinger et al. (in review) and regional CCVA studies for its climate science content. The plan's primary analytical work is the SGCN scoring system, habitat threat/action tables, and Conservation Opportunity Area delineation.

evidence_index.text: Climate change vulnerability is comprised of three separate but related components -exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Exposure is a reflection of the type, degree, and duration of climate induced change. The degree to which the effects of that change are felt is related to the sensitivity of the object being acted upon. Adaptive capacity is a measure of object's ability to persist in the face of the change.

orientation.summary: This is the 2025 Oklahoma State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP), a strategic-level conservation plan for the state of Oklahoma that identifies Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN), their essential habitats, conservation issues, and recommended actions. The document engages with climate change in a dedicated 'Climate Adaptation' section that discusses IPCC scenarios (RCPs, SSPs), climate projections from SC-CASC/NOAA/Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory, and potential strategies for resistance, resilience, and adaptability. It acknowledges range shifts explicitly ('Some species may expand or contract their geographic ranges northward in response to temperature shifts or eastward in response to rainfall shifts') and discusses connectivity, habitat loss, invasive species, and aquatic vulnerability in climate terms. The plan primarily references external analyses (e.g., SECAS Blueprint connectivity analysis, climate projections generated by SC-CASC) rather than performing new modeling itself, though it incorporates the results of those analyses into its spatial prioritization and conservation actions.

evidence_index.text: Some species may expand or contract their geographic ranges northward in response to temperature shifts or eastward in response to rainfall shifts.

Scientists use global climate models (GCMs) to project future climate conditions and assess the direction and magnitude of change over time. More than two dozen of these models have been examined by the IPCC and run through different scenarios that vary in terms of projected human population growth, economic and technological development and greenhouse gas emissions.

The AR6 uses two primary sets of scenarios known as representative concentration pathways (RCPs) and shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs). Three RCPs are outlined in the AR6: RCP2.6, RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. Similarly, five SSPs are identified in the AR6: SSP1-1.9, SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5.

Projections for Oklahoma were generated through SC-CASC and the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory of NOAA. The historical annual average daytime high of Oklahoma is 72.1°F. Average annual high temperatures for the period from 2036-2065 (mid-century) are projected to increase by about 2°F for the low-end scenario to about 5°F for the high-end scenario above the historical annual average high temperatures.

Adaptability (also referred to as adaptive capacity) contains elements of resilience and also includes the ability of species to change genetically, temporally, spatially, or behaviorally in response to environmental change.

Resilience is the ability of a population or a community, or an ecological process, to recover or maintain a new stable state after disturbance. Often, management to increase resilience involves actions that increase structural diversity in a system or genetic diversity within a population.

Increase habitat connectivity. Greater connectivity between tracts of habitat increases dispersal of both plant and animal species and connects neighboring populations in a metapopulational fashion. Connectivity reduces the isolation of populations and helps to maintain the genetic diversity that helps populations adapt to change. Habitat connectivity also assists in movement of populations across the landscape and allows them to track changes and shift their range.

Expand the size of habitat tracts. Larger tracts of habitat can support larger populations of plants and animals and can serve as refugia. Larger populations are often more robust and better able to resist the negative effects of population isolation, fluctuations in reproductive success due to climate variables, and competition from invading species.

Focus on areas with a high degree of topographic relief. Mountainous areas tend to be more resilient to climate change because their varied topographic relief can support many microhabitat conditions and an elevational gradient that facilitates the easy movement of plants and animals upward or downward in response to changes in temperature or rainfall.

Aquatic communities are likely to be more negatively affected by changes in climate than many terrestrial communities. Restoring, enhancing, and conserving existing riparian forests and other native flood plain habitats will help to shade streams, protect flood plain... aquatic communities such as those found in the Ozark Highlands are especially vulnerable to change.
